metadata.title: Idaho v. Coeur D'Alene Tribe of Idaho, 521 U.S. 261 (1997) (No. 94-1474)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Idaho v. Coeur D'Alene Tribe of Idaho

Opinion filed: 1997-06-23

Docket No.: 94-1474

Citations:
• 138 L. Ed. 2d 438
• 117 S. Ct. 2028
• 521 U.S. 261
• 1997 U.S. LEXIS 4030

Case holding summaries:
• “The real interests served by the Eleventh Amendment are not to be sacrificed to elementary mechanics of captions and pleading.”
• stating that "navigable waters uniquely implicate [a state's] sovereign interests"
• "We do not . . . question the continuing validity of the Ex parte Young doctrine."
• principal opinion of Kennedy, J., joined by Rehnquist, C.J.
• O’Connor, J., joined by Scalia and Thomas, JJ., concurring in part and concurring in judgment
• affirming that, in applying Ex parte Young, courts “must ensure that the doctrine of sovereign immunity remains meaningful, while also giving recognition to the need to prevent violations of federal law”
• Young doctrine "a basic principle of federal law"
• noting that “Eleventh Amendment immunity represents a real limitation on a federal court’s federal-question jurisdiction.”
• “The real interests served by the Eleventh Amendment are not to be sacrificed to elementary mechanics of captions and pleading.”
• O'Connor, J., concurring in part and concurring in the judgment(joined by Scalia and Thomas, JJ.)
• noting that the "Court's recognition of sovereign immunity has not been limited to the suits described in the text of the Eleventh Amendment"
• a state cannot be sued in federal court without its consent
• “When suit is commenced against state officials, even if they are named and served as individuals, the State itself will have a continuing interest in the litigation whenever state policies or procedures are at stake.”
• O'Connor, J., joined by Scalia and Thomas, JJ., concurring in part and concurring in judgment
• reaffirming that a plaintiff seeking prospective relief against a state official’s ongoing violation of federal law can proceed in federal court
• referring to the "particular and special circumstances" of the case
• "The Amendment, in other words, enacts a sover- eign immunity from suit, rather than a nonwaivable limit on the federal judiciary's subject-matter jurisdiction."
• so noting as to Eleventh Amendment immunity of states
• "I would not narrow our Young doctrine."
• holding that the state had a unique sovereign interest in submerged land within its borders, and therefore state officials could not be sued even under Ex parte Young
• "[T]he inadequacy of a legal remedy is a prerequisite for equitable relief in any case."
• “Our precedents do teach us, nevertheless, that where prospective relief is sought against individual state officers in a federal forum based on a federal right, the Eleventh Amendment, in most cases, is not a bar.” (emphasis added)
• recognizing that the Ex parte Young doctrine extends to violations of federal law
• distinguishing Eleventh Amendment immunity from defects in subject matter jurisdiction
• "The Young doctrine recognizes that if a state official violates federal law, he is stripped of his official or representative character and may be personally liable for his conduct; the State cannot cloak the officer in its sovereign immunity."
• “State ownership of [submerged lands] has been considered an essential attribute of sovereignty.”
• barring a suit that was equivalent to a quiet title suit
• " Ex parte Young gives life to the Supremacy Clause." (quoting Green v. Mansour, 474 U.S. 64, 68, 106 S.Ct. 423, 88 L.Ed.2d 371 (1985))
• state immunity statute cannot immunize an officer from a § 1983 suit in state court
• common-law tort of injuring plaintiff's reputation and sale of certain products
• discussing the "enormous and overwhelming" penalties for violating the challenged statutes
• common-law tort of patent infringement
• penalties for each violation of the challenged statute included $1,000 fine
• rejecting proposed rule that would relegate certain § 1983 claims to state court in the face of the statute's basic policy of providing a federal forum for vindication of federal rights
• stating that the State's interest in the suit was so "direct" that "perhaps no decree ought to have been pronounced in the cause, until the State was before the court"
• concluding that Title VII's authorization of federal-court jurisdiction to award money damages against a state government to individuals subjected to employment discrimination does not violate the Eleventh Amendment since Congress was exercising its § 5 remedial powers
• penalties for violating the challenged statute could "in a short time . . . amount to many thousands of dollars"
• explaining that if it was within the power of the plaintiff to make the State a party to the suit it would "certainly [be] true" that a suit against state officials would be barred, but if the "real principal" is "exempt from all judicial process" an officer suit could proceed
• penalties for violations are "such as might well deter even the boldest and most confident"
• "Because of the local ill feeling, the people of the States where [the Indians] are found are often their deadliest enemies"
• "[I]t cannot be doubted that the question whether a particular suit is one against the State, within the meaning of the Constitution, must depend upon the same principles that determine whether a particular suit is one against the United States"
• explaining that the state-law remedy for Virginia's unconstitutional refusal to accept its own bond coupons in satisfaction of state taxes was, in fact, "no remedy"
• Eleventh Amendment bars notice relief where plaintiffs alleged no ongoing violation of federal law
• Young `s applicability "is to be determined not by the mere names of the titular parties but by the essential nature and effect of the proceeding, as it appears from the entire record"
• permitting suit for injunctive relief to proceed where there did not otherwise exist a legal remedy for the alleged trespass
• "[T]he government is always at liberty, notwithstanding any such judgment, to avail itself of all the remedies which the law allows to every person, natural or artificial, for the vindication and assertion of its rights"
• noting that Young rests on a fictional distinction between the official and the State
• "[T]he Young doctrine has been accepted as necessary to permit the federal courts to vindicate federal rights" (citation omitted)
• plaintiff cannot invoke Young doctrine based solely on alleged violation of state law
• a "federal court, consistent with the Eleventh Amendment, may enjoin state officials to conform their future conduct to the requirements of federal law, even though such an injunction may have an ancillary effect on the state treasury"
